lead: Offshore every heading and bearing passes through a compass you must trust; a fix is as good as its worst line.

sections.title: Lubber line, liquid, variation

qa.q: How do I bring the variation on an old chart up to this year?
qa.a: Multiply the rose's **annual change** by the years since its date and apply it: 4°10'W in 2016, changing 8'E a year, is 2°50'W in 2026.

refs: Compass — variation and its annual change

blocks.p: A compass reads the heading if its **lubber line** is parallel to the fore-and-aft line. A bubble makes the card stick and jump: cross-check against another compass, refill ashore. After a hard turn the liquid drags the card; log the heading once it settles. Keep gear outside its **compass safe distance**; a loudspeaker needs the most.

**Variation** comes from the nearest rose or, on a small-scale sheet, the isogonic line, updated by its annual change; a long leg crosses several. **Heeling error**, iron below the compass tilting with the boat, is largest heading north or south: check the deviation heeled.

sections.title: The swing and the card

qa.q: How do I check my compass deviation at sea?
qa.a: On a steady heading, compare the compass with a known magnetic direction: a transit, the sun's or Polaris's tabled azimuth, or a satellite compass, never COG. A compass reading low has easterly **deviation**.

refs: Compass — deviation card from a swing
Compass — swinging on a distant mark
Compass — deviation by the sun's azimuth
Compass — deviation by the Pole Star
Compass — bearings on a steel yacht

blocks.p: **Deviation** is the boat's own magnetism; it changes with the heading, so the card lists it heading by heading, and each compass has its own. Find it on a steady heading against a known magnetic direction: a transit, the sun's or Polaris's tabled azimuth, a satellite compass; never COG, which a current sets off the heading. A compass reading low has easterly deviation.

fig.title: Deviation by azimuth: worked example
lines: Heading steady 165°C; sun over the pin 119°C
Swing on a far peak: mean of 8 bearings 222°
That mean is magnetic; on 090°C it read 218°

blocks.p: Large deviation calls for an **adjuster** and a new swing. A steel hull changes her magnetism after a winter bow-north, welding or hours on one heading; new wiring or instruments by the compass change it too: swing again. On steel take bearings over the steering compass. A fresh check that disagrees with the card is logged and used.

sections.title: Fluxgate, satellite compass, COG

qa.q: Can I use GPS COG instead of a heading sensor for radar overlay?
qa.a: No: **COG** is your track over the ground, not a heading, so it is no good for radar overlay or MARPA. A satellite compass gives true heading, even stopped.

refs: Electronic compass — heading error at speed

head: Source
Gives
Weakness
rows: Iron, cables, tilt in a turn
Not a heading: no good for overlay or MARPA

blocks.p: Calibration circles take out a fluxgate's deviation, not an alignment error: set the offset after a transit check. Mount it low, central, clear of iron. A **satellite compass** needs no card and feeds autopilot, radar and AIS. The magnetic compass keeps its card and, under jamming, is the only heading left.

sections.title: What each line tells you

qa.q: In what order should I take bearings for a three-point fix?
qa.a: Slow-changing bearings ahead and astern first, the beam one last, with the lines crossing near **right angles**. A cocked hat the size the errors give is honest: treat it as an area.

refs: Position fixing — transit and a second line
Position fixing — depth and a bearing

blocks.p: A position line fixes you across itself, not along it: a bearing of the light ahead checks the cross-track error, a contour across the track checks the distance run, a sounding helps where contours cross your line. Take bearings near right angles, slow-changing ones ahead and astern first, the beam one last. 3° at 20 M is 1 M.

fig.note: The arcs cross twice: even a rough bearing picks X

head: Line

rows: ±1–2°; head-up adds the heading; land paints half a beamwidth wide
Weak beyond 3× the spacing · range to the flash's inner end
Same deviation in each: the same cocked hat every time

blocks.p: A **cocked hat** the size the errors give is honest: treat it as an area. Horizontal sextant angles need no compass. Fix on charted lighthouses, not aero lights or flare stacks; AIS targets come from your own GNSS. A soft echo far down is plankton; soundings at equal intervals, on tracing paper slid over the chart, fix you offshore.

sections.title: Two bearings of one mark

qa.q: How do I get a fix from two bearings of the same light?
qa.a: By a **running fix**: take a bearing, run on, take a second, and move the first line along the ground run, water legs and stream added as vectors. Where the lines cut is the fix.

refs: Position fixing — doubling the angle on the bow

blocks.p: With one mark: a bearing, a run, a second bearing, and the first line moved by the **ground run**: water legs and hours of stream added as vectors. A range circle moves by its centre, a contour likewise. The fix is as good as the run: 0.4 kn of doubt over 2.5 h is 1 M.

fig.note: Four-point bearing: abeam, the distance off equals the run

fig.title: Running fix with stream
lines: 0300: light bears 330°T; the cut is the fix

blocks.p: They need the ground run on a steady course: a stream along the track goes into the run; a cross-set breaks them: plot.

qa.q: At what distance will a lighthouse rise above the horizon?
qa.a: At its **rising range**, 2.08 × (√H + √h) miles with heights in metres, within its nominal range. The charted height is above MHWS, so at low water add the tide's fall.

blocks.p: A light rises at 2.08 × (√H + √h) miles, within its nominal range; its charted height is above MHWS, so add the tide's fall at low water. Seen only from the crests, it is on your horizon, at its rising range. Abnormal refraction shows it far beyond. Card each expected light: characteristic, rising range, bearing. One 15–20° off may still be yours if the EP is miles out: time it. Nothing after rising time: an obscured sector. A colour change puts you on the sector's edge.

fig.note: Seen only from the crests: you stand at its rising range

fig.title: Rising range and distance off

H = 40 + 3.0 = 43 m; height of eye 4 m
24 M to go at 11 kn: it rises in 34 min
Vertical sextant angle 0°20.0' of the 43 m:

blocks.p: A **vertical sextant angle**, light to the shoreline below it, gives 1.854 × H ÷ angle in minutes, index error applied, tide added to H.

sections.title: Believing a fix, recording it

qa.q: How do I check that my GPS position is right?
qa.a: Against something independent: depth, radar, lights or, offshore, the EP from the last fix. Plotter, AIS and DSC share one **receiver**, so their agreement proves nothing.

refs: Position fixing — which fix to trust
Recording fixes — a single position line

blocks.p: Plotter, AIS and DSC share one receiver: their agreement proves nothing; nor does HDOP without RAIM. Cross-check against depth, radar, lights or, offshore, the EP from the last fix. Jumps, a frozen speed or a wrong date mean spoofing: back to DR from the last non-GNSS fix. A visual fix 0.5 M from the GNSS at 20 M agrees; hand bearings beside steel share one error.

fig.note: Put yourself on the line at the point nearest the EP

blocks.p: Fix hourly in open water, and before the EP's doubt, about 10% of the run, reaches half the gap to a bank. Keep a single line: plot it with its time, log the bearing and the log.
